All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

7	There are two genuinely different parts: constructing counterexamples below \(1/9\), and proving that every \(c>1/9\) works.

9	I give both proofs. The only general theorems used are the classical **Szemerédi regularity lemma** and **Kneser’s theorem**
10	\[
11	\chi\bigl(KG(m,k)\bigr)=m-2k+2.
12	\]
13	No homomorphism-threshold theorem is used as a black box.
14	
15	## 1. Replacing the homomorphism problem by a coloring problem
16	
17	For a triangle-free graph \(G\), let \(P(G)\) be the graph on \(V(G)\) in which two vertices are adjacent if there is a walk of length three between them.
18	
19	There are no loops in \(P(G)\), since a closed walk of length three would be a triangle. Also, every edge of \(G\) is an edge of \(P(G)\), by backtracking.
20	
21	### Lemma 1
22	For every positive integer \(q\), there is a finite triangle-free graph \(U_q\) such that
23	\[
24	\chi(P(G))\le q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\longrightarrow U_q.
25	\]
26	
27	**Proof.** The vertices of \(U_q\) are the pairs
28	\[
29	(i,S),\qquad i\in[q],\quad S\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\}.
30	\]
31	Put an edge between \((i,S)\) and \((j,T)\) precisely when
32	\[
33	i\in T,\qquad j\in S,\qquad S\cap T=\varnothing.
34	\]
35	
36	This graph is triangle-free. Indeed, if \((i,S),(j,T),(k,W)\) formed a triangle, adjacency to the first vertex would give
37	\[
38	i\in T\cap W,
39	\]
40	contradicting adjacency between the other two vertices.
41	
42	Now take a proper \(q\)-coloring \(a\) of \(P(G)\), and define
43	\[
44	f(v)=\bigl(a(v),\{a(w):w\in N_G(v)\}\bigr).
45	\]
46	For \(uv\in E(G)\), the required cross-memberships hold. The two sets of neighbor-colors are disjoint: otherwise there would be \(x\in N(u)\), \(y\in N(v)\) with \(a(x)=a(y)\), although \(x,u,v,y\) is a length-three walk. The possibility \(x=y\) would itself give a triangle in \(G\). Thus \(f\) is a homomorphism. ∎
47	
48	We will also repeatedly use the following elementary observation:
49	\[
50	\boxed{\text{If \(G\) has no \(C_3,C_5\), and \(xy\in E(P(G))\), then }
51	N_G(x)\cap N_G(y)=\varnothing.} \tag{1}
52	\]
53	Otherwise a length-three walk from \(x\) to \(y\), followed by a common neighbor, gives a closed odd walk of length five. Every such walk contains a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## 2. The lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails
58	
59	Fix \(c<1/9\), and let \(H\) be any finite triangle-free graph. Write \(h=|V(H)|\), assuming \(h\ge1\).
60	
61	Choose an integer \(k\) sufficiently large that
62	\[
63	\frac{k}{9k+3h}>c,
64	\]
65	and put
66	\[
67	m=2k+h,\qquad F=KG(m,k).
68	\]
69	Thus vertices of \(F\) are the \(k\)-subsets of \([m]\), adjacent when disjoint. Kneser’s theorem gives
70	\[
71	\chi(F)=m-2k+2=h+2>h. \tag{2}
72	\]
73	
74	### 2.1 A sparsely subdivided core
75	
76	Orient every edge of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace each oriented edge \(S\to T\) by
77	\[
78	x_S-a_{ST}-b_{ST}-x_T.
79	\]
80	Call the resulting graph \(Q\). Partition its vertices into three independent sets:
81	\[
82	Q_0=\{x_S\},\qquad Q_1=\{a_{ST}\},\qquad Q_2=\{b_{ST}\}.
83	\]
84	Assign each vertex a \(k\)-element label:
85	\[
86	L(x_S)=S,\qquad L(a_{ST})=S,\qquad L(b_{ST})=T.
87	\]
88	
89	These labels have the crucial property
90	\[
91	u,v\in Q_i,\ uv\in E(P(Q))
92	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(u)\cap L(v)=\varnothing. \tag{3}
93	\]
94	
95	To verify this, a length-three walk with both ends in the same class must traverse the three classes cyclically.
96	
97	* In \(Q_0\), its ends correspond to an edge \(ST\) of \(F\).
98	* In \(Q_1\) or \(Q_2\), it comes from two consecutively oriented edges of \(F\), in one direction or the other.
99	
100	In each case the two labels are endpoints of an edge of \(F\), hence are disjoint.
101	
102	Also, \(Q\) has no cycle shorter than nine: it is the three-subdivision of a simple graph.
103	
104	### 2.2 Adding dense reservoirs
105	
106	Choose a positive integer \(t\). For each \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
107	
108	* \(R_i=[m]\times[t]\), of size \(mt\);
109	* an independent set \(Z_i\), of size \(kt\);
110	* all edges between \(R_i\) and \(Z_i\);
111	* for \(v\in Q_i\), all edges from \(v\) to
112	  \[
113	  L(v)\times[t]\subseteq R_i.
114	  \]
115	
116	There are no other edges. Denote this graph by \(G_t\).
117	
118	Every vertex has degree at least \(kt\):
119	
120	* each core vertex has \(kt\) reservoir neighbors;
121	* each vertex of \(R_i\) has all \(kt\) neighbors in \(Z_i\);
122	* each vertex of \(Z_i\) has \(mt\ge kt\) neighbors in \(R_i\).
123	
124	Writing \(s=|V(Q)|\), we obtain
125	\[
126	|V(G_t)|=s+3(m+k)t
127	\]
128	and
129	\[
130	\frac{\delta(G_t)}{|V(G_t)|}
131	\ge
132	\frac{kt}{s+3(m+k)t}
133	\longrightarrow
134	\frac{k}{3(m+k)}
135	=
136	\frac{k}{9k+3h}>c. \tag{4}
137	\]
138	Thus sufficiently large \(t\) gives the required minimum degree.
139	
140	### 2.3 Checking the forbidden cycles
141	
142	There are no \(3\)- or \(5\)-cycles wholly inside \(Q\).
143	
144	A \(5\)-cycle containing a vertex of \(Z_i\) would have the form
145	\[
146	Z_i-R_i-Q_i-Q_i-R_i-Z_i,
147	\]
148	forcing an edge inside \(Q_i\), which is impossible. A triangle containing \(Z_i\) is also impossible.
149	
150	Consider a short odd cycle containing reservoir vertices but no \(Z_i\).
151	
152	* A triangle would force an edge inside some \(Q_i\).
153	* A \(5\)-cycle with one reservoir vertex would give a length-three path in \(Q\), with ends in the same \(Q_i\) whose labels have a common element. This contradicts (3).
154	* A \(5\)-cycle with two reservoir vertices has the form
155	  \[
156	  r-x-r'-y-z-r.
157	  \]
158	  The common neighbor \(x\) forces \(r,r'\in R_i\) for the same \(i\); then \(y,z\in Q_i\), again forcing an edge inside \(Q_i\).
159	
160	Hence \(G_t\) has no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\).
161	
162	### 2.4 Why it cannot map to \(H\)
163	
164	Suppose \(f:G_t\to H\) were a homomorphism. For every edge \(ST\) of \(F\), its subdivided path gives a length-three walk in \(H\) from \(f(x_S)\) to \(f(x_T)\).
165	
166	These two endpoints cannot be equal, since \(H\) is triangle-free. Therefore
167	\[
168	S\longmapsto f(x_S)
169	\]
170	would properly color \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors, contradicting (2).
171	
172	Thus every \(c<1/9\) fails.
173

176	## 3. The upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
177	
178	Fix \(c>1/9\), and set
179	\[
180	\tau=\frac{c-1/9}{10}.
181	\]
182	In particular,
183	\[
184	9c-15\tau>1. \tag{5}
185	\]
186	
187	We prove that \(\chi(P(G))\) is bounded in terms of \(c\).
188	
189	### 3.1 The regularity setup
190	
191	We need the following standard consequence of the regularity lemma.
192	
193	### Regularity consequence
194	For fixed \(c,\tau>0\), and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), every sufficiently large graph with minimum degree at least \(cn\) has a partition
195	\[
196	V(G)=V_0\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_k
197	\]
198	such that:
199	
200	1. \(|V_0|\le\tau n\);
201	2. \(|V_1|=\cdots=|V_k|=M\);
202	3. \(k\le K\), where \(K\) depends only on the fixed parameters;
203	4. there is a reduced graph \(R\) on \([k]\) with
204	   \[
205	   \delta(R)\ge(c-\tau)k, \tag{6}
206	   \]
207	   whose edges represent \(\varepsilon\)-regular pairs of density at least \(d=\tau/4\).
208	
209	Here \(\varepsilon\) can be chosen as small as needed relative to \(\tau,d\).
210	
211	For completeness, the minimum-degree assertion follows by starting with a much finer regularity parameter \(\eta\). Move to \(V_0\) every cluster incident with more than \(\sqrt\eta\,k\) irregular pairs; at most \(2\sqrt\eta\,k\) clusters are moved. Discard irregular pairs and pairs of density below \(d\). For each remaining cluster, average its vertices’ degrees. The losses are at most
212	\[
213	d+O(\sqrt\eta)+O(1/k)
214	\]
215	as a proportion of all clusters. Taking \(\eta\) sufficiently small and the initial number of clusters sufficiently large gives (6), as well as \(|V_0|\le\tau n\).
216	
217	For each vertex \(v\in V(G)\), define its **profile**
218	\[
219	I(v)=\{i\in[k]: |N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\tau M\}.
220	\]
221	There are at most \(2^K\) profiles.
222	
223	The number of neighbors of \(v\) outside the clusters indexed by \(I(v)\) is at most
224	\[
225	|V_0|+\tau kM\le2\tau n. \tag{7}
226	\]
227	Consequently every occurring profile is nonempty.
228	
229	### 3.2 Three restrictions on profiles
230	
231	Write \(N_R(I)=\bigcup_{i\in I}N_R(i)\). Regularity and the absence of \(C_3,C_5\) give:
232	
233	\[
234	\begin{array}{ll}
235	\text{(A)} & I(v)\text{ is independent in }R;\\[2mm]
236	\text{(B)} & uv\in E(G)\Longrightarrow
237	N_R(I(u))\cap N_R(I(v))=\varnothing;\\[2mm]
238	\text{(C)} & u-w-v\text{ is a length-two walk in }G\\
239	&\hspace{13mm}\Longrightarrow
240	\text{there is no \(R\)-edge between }I(u)\text{ and }I(v).
241	\end{array} \tag{8}
242	\]
243	
244	Here are the embedding details.
245	
246	* An \(R\)-edge between two clusters in \(I(v)\) supplies an edge between two neighbors of \(v\), giving a triangle.
247	* If \(uv\in E(G)\) and some reduced vertex is adjacent to a cluster in \(I(u)\) and a cluster in \(I(v)\), regularity supplies a length-two path between a neighbor of \(u\) and a neighbor of \(v\). Together with \(uv\), this is a \(5\)-cycle.
248	* An \(R\)-edge between clusters in \(I(u)\) and \(I(v)\), together with \(u-w-v\), similarly gives a \(5\)-cycle. If \(u=v\), use (A).
249	
250	These applications only involve endpoint subsets of size at least \(\tau M\). Taking \(\varepsilon\ll\tau,d\) guarantees the requisite edges. For the length-two path, all but at most \(2\varepsilon M\) vertices in its middle cluster have many neighbors in both prescribed endpoint subsets. Taking \(M\) sufficiently large allows all previously specified vertices to be avoided, so the cycles are genuine subgraphs.
251	
252	### 3.3 Profiles containing an edge of \(P(G)\) are large
253	
254	Suppose \(x,y\) have the same profile \(I\) and \(xy\in E(P(G))\). By (1), their neighborhoods are disjoint. By (7), each has at least \((c-2\tau)n\) neighbors in the clusters of \(I\). Hence
255	\[
256	|I|M\ge2(c-2\tau)n,
257	\]
258	and therefore
259	\[
260	|I|\ge2(c-2\tau)k. \tag{9}
261	\]
262	
263	### 3.4 A six-set packing argument
264	
265	Fix an occurring profile \(I\), and let \(F_I\) be the subgraph of \(P(G)\) induced by the vertices with profile \(I\).
266	
267	Orient every edge of \(F_I\) according to any fixed vertex ordering. For each oriented edge \(x\to y\), choose a witnessing length-three walk
268	\[
269	x-a-b-y
270	\]
271	and give that oriented edge the color
272	\[
273	\bigl(I(a),I(b)\bigr).
274	\]
275	There are at most
276	\[
277	(2^K)^2
278	\]
279	colors.
280	
281	We claim that no color class contains a directed length-two path.
282	
283	Suppose otherwise. We have two witnesses
284	\[
285	x-a-b-y,\qquad y-a'-b'-z
286	\]
287	whose profile sequences are
288	\[
289	I,J,L,I,\qquad I,J,L,I.
290	\]
291	
292	From the three edges of the first witness, (B) gives pairwise disjointness of
293	\[
294	N_R(I),\quad N_R(J),\quad N_R(L). \tag{10}
295	\]
296	
297	From the length-two walks
298	\[
299	x-a-b,\qquad a-b-y,\qquad b-y-a',
300	\]
301	condition (C) says that there are no reduced edges between any two of \(I,J,L\). Each is itself independent by (A). Thus
302	\[
303	I\cup J\cup L\text{ is independent in }R. \tag{11}
304	\]
305	
306	Since \(R\) has positive minimum degree, (10) also forces \(I,J,L\) to be pairwise disjoint: a reduced vertex in two of them would have a neighbor lying in two of the sets in (10).
307	
308	It follows from (10)–(11) that the six sets
309	\[
310	I,\ J,\ L,\ N_R(I),\ N_R(J),\ N_R(L)
311	\]
312	are pairwise disjoint.
313	
314	Moreover, each of \(I,J,L\) contains the ends of an edge of \(P(G)\):
315	
316	* \(x,y\) have profile \(I\);
317	* \(a,b,y,a'\) is a length-three walk with endpoint profile \(J\);
318	* \(b,y,a',b'\) is one with endpoint profile \(L\).
319	
320	The endpoints in these walks are distinct; otherwise there would be a triangle. Applying (9), and then (6), gives
321	\[
322	\begin{aligned}
323	k
324	&\ge |I|+|J|+|L|
325	   +|N_R(I)|+|N_R(J)|+|N_R(L)|\\
326	&\ge 6(c-2\tau)k+3(c-\tau)k\\
327	&=(9c-15\tau)k\\
328	&>k,
329	\end{aligned}
330	\]
331	a contradiction.
332	
333	This proves the claim.
334	
335	An oriented graph containing no directed length-two path is bipartite: every nonisolated vertex is exclusively a source or exclusively a sink. Therefore every color class in \(F_I\) is bipartite.
336	
337	A graph whose edges are the union of \(r\) bipartite graphs is \(2^r\)-colorable, by recording one bipartition bit for each graph. Consequently, with \(T=2^K\),
338	\[
339	\chi(F_I)\le2^{T^2}
340	\]
341	and
342	\[
343	\chi(P(G))\le T\,2^{T^2}. \tag{12}
344	\]
345	
346	This bound depends only on \(c\). Graphs below the fixed size required by the regularity argument can be accommodated by increasing the bound.
347	
348	Lemma 1 now supplies a single finite triangle-free target for all such \(G\). Thus every \(c>1/9\) works.
349	
350	Together with the lower bound, this proves the claimed infimum.
351	
352	---
353	
354	## 4. Python verification
355	
356	The following is executable Python, using NumPy, NetworkX and Z3. It checks:
357	
358	* explicit instances of the lower-bound construction;
359	* the absence of \(C_3,C_5\), using exact integer closed-walk counts;
360	* the same-class label condition;
361	* small Kneser chromatic numbers, independently with Z3;
362	* a nonexistence-of-homomorphism instance;
363	* the universal-target reduction on **all 172 triangle-free graphs in NetworkX’s atlas**;
364	* exact arithmetic for counterexample parameters arbitrarily close to \(1/9\).
365	
366	The finite checks supplement, rather than replace, the proofs of the infinite assertions.

13	## 1. Replacing the homomorphism problem by a coloring problem
14	
15	For a triangle-free graph \(G\), let \(P(G)\) be the graph on \(V(G)\) in which two vertices are adjacent if there is a walk of length three between them.
16	
17	There are no loops in \(P(G)\), since a closed walk of length three would be a triangle. Also, every edge of \(G\) is an edge of \(P(G)\), by backtracking.
18	
19	### Lemma 1
20	For every positive integer \(q\), there is a finite triangle-free graph \(U_q\) such that
21	\[
22	\chi(P(G))\le q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\longrightarrow U_q.
23	\]
24	
25	**Proof.** The vertices of \(U_q\) are the pairs
26	\[
27	(i,S),\qquad i\in[q],\quad S\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\}.
28	\]
29	Put an edge between \((i,S)\) and \((j,T)\) precisely when
30	\[
31	i\in T,\qquad j\in S,\qquad S\cap T=\varnothing.
32	\]

34	This graph is triangle-free. Indeed, if \((i,S),(j,T),(k,W)\) formed a triangle, adjacency to the first vertex would give
35	\[

37	\]
38	contradicting adjacency between the other two vertices.

40	Now take a proper \(q\)-coloring \(a\) of \(P(G)\), and define
41	\[
42	f(v)=\bigl(a(v),\{a(w):w\in N_G(v)\}\bigr).

191	### Regularity consequence
192	For fixed \(c,\tau>0\), and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), every sufficiently large graph with minimum degree at least \(cn\) has a partition
193	\[
194	V(G)=V_0\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_k

198	1. \(|V_0|\le\tau n\);
199	2. \(|V_1|=\cdots=|V_k|=M\);
200	3. \(k\le K\), where \(K\) depends only on the fixed parameters;
201	4. there is a reduced graph \(R\) on \([k]\) with
202	   \[
203	   \delta(R)\ge(c-\tau)k, \tag{6}
204	   \]
205	   whose edges represent \(\varepsilon\)-regular pairs of density at least \(d=\tau/4\).

207	Here \(\varepsilon\) can be chosen as small as needed relative to \(\tau,d\).
208	
209	For completeness, the minimum-degree assertion follows by starting with a much finer regularity parameter \(\eta\). Move to \(V_0\) every cluster incident with more than \(\sqrt\eta\,k\) irregular pairs; at most \(2\sqrt\eta\,k\) clusters are moved. Discard irregular pairs and pairs of density below \(d\). For each remaining cluster, average its vertices’ degrees. The losses are at most
210	\[
211	d+O(\sqrt\eta)+O(1/k)
212	\]
213	as a proportion of all clusters. Taking \(\eta\) sufficiently small and the initial number of clusters sufficiently large gives (6), as well as \(|V_0|\le\tau n\).
214	
215	For each vertex \(v\in V(G)\), define its **profile**
216	\[
217	I(v)=\{i\in[k]: |N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\tau M\}.
218	\]
219	There are at most \(2^K\) profiles.
220	
221	The number of neighbors of \(v\) outside the clusters indexed by \(I(v)\) is at most
222	\[
223	|V_0|+\tau kM\le2\tau n. \tag{7}
224	\]
225	Consequently every occurring profile is nonempty.

227	### 3.2 Three restrictions on profiles
228	
229	Write \(N_R(I)=\bigcup_{i\in I}N_R(i)\). Regularity and the absence of \(C_3,C_5\) give:
230	
231	\[
232	\begin{array}{ll}
233	\text{(A)} & I(v)\text{ is independent in }R;\\[2mm]
234	\text{(B)} & uv\in E(G)\Longrightarrow
235	N_R(I(u))\cap N_R(I(v))=\varnothing;\\[2mm]
236	\text{(C)} & u-w-v\text{ is a length-two walk in }G\\
237	&\hspace{13mm}\Longrightarrow
238	\text{there is no \(R\)-edge between }I(u)\text{ and }I(v).
239	\end{array} \tag{8}
240	\]
241	
242	Here are the embedding details.
243	
244	* An \(R\)-edge between two clusters in \(I(v)\) supplies an edge between two neighbors of \(v\), giving a triangle.
245	* If \(uv\in E(G)\) and some reduced vertex is adjacent to a cluster in \(I(u)\) and a cluster in \(I(v)\), regularity supplies a length-two path between a neighbor of \(u\) and a neighbor of \(v\). Together with \(uv\), this is a \(5\)-cycle.
246	* An \(R\)-edge between clusters in \(I(u)\) and \(I(v)\), together with \(u-w-v\), similarly gives a \(5\)-cycle. If \(u=v\), use (A).

248	These applications only involve endpoint subsets of size at least \(\tau M\). Taking \(\varepsilon\ll\tau,d\) guarantees the requisite edges. 263	Fix an occurring profile \(I\), and let \(F_I\) be the subgraph of \(P(G)\) induced by the vertices with profile \(I\).
